questions.enonce_markdown:
The vector equations of two lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ are

$$L_1: \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}) + \lambda(\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}),$$

$$L_2: \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}) + \mu(\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{k}),$$

where $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are scalar variables.

Find

(a) the values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ for which $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect, stating the position vector of the point of intersection. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write the lines in components:

$$L_1: \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda \\ 1 + 2\lambda \\ -1 + \lambda \end{pmatrix}, \qquad L_2: \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + \mu \\ 7 \\ -4 + 3\mu \end{pmatrix}.$$

At an intersection the two position vectors are equal, so equate the $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ components:

$$\mathbf{i}: \; \lambda = 1 + \mu, \qquad \mathbf{j}: \; 1 + 2\lambda = 7, \qquad \mathbf{k}: \; -1 + \lambda = -4 + 3\mu.$$

From the $\mathbf{j}$ equation, $2\lambda = 6$, so $\lambda = 3$. From the $\mathbf{i}$ equation, $\mu = \lambda - 1 = 2$.

Check in the $\mathbf{k}$ equation (the third, unused equation): left side $-1 + 3 = 2$; right side $-4 + 3(2) = 2$. They agree, so the lines really do intersect (they are not skew).

$$\boxed{\lambda = 3, \qquad \mu = 2}$$

Position vector of the point of intersection (put $\lambda = 3$ in $L_1$): $\mathbf{r} = (0 + 3)\mathbf{i} + (1 + 6)\mathbf{j} + (-1 + 3)\mathbf{k}$.

$$\boxed{\mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}}$$

Check with $L_2$, $\mu = 2$: $(1 + 2)\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j} + (-4 + 6)\mathbf{k} = 3\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$. Same point.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) the Cartesian equation of the plane containing $L_1$ and $L_2$. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Normal vector.** The plane contains both lines, so its normal $\mathbf{n}$ is perpendicular to both direction vectors $\mathbf{d}_1 = \mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{d}_2 = \mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{k}$. Take the vector product:

$$\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = (6 - 0)\mathbf{i} - (3 - 1)\mathbf{j} + (0 - 2)\mathbf{k} = 6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} - 2\mathbf{k}.$$

Divide by $2$: a normal vector is $3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}$.

**Equation.** The plane has equation $\mathbf{r}\cdot(3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}) = d$, i.e. $3x - y - z = d$. It passes through the point of intersection $(3, 7, 2)$:

$$d = 3(3) - 7 - 2 = 0.$$

$$\boxed{3x - y - z = 0}$$

Check with other points of the lines: $(0, 1, -1)$ on $L_1$: $0 - 1 + 1 = 0$. Correct. $(1, 7, -4)$ on $L_2$: $3 - 7 + 4 = 0$. Correct. Also $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_1 = 3 - 2 - 1 = 0$ and $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_2 = 3 - 3 = 0$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A bus driver has $8$ passengers to carry but he only has room for $4$.

In how many ways can he choose the $4$ passengers, if two of them are sisters who must not be separated. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Interpretation: the two sisters must not be separated, so **either both are chosen, or neither is chosen** (one sister may not travel without the other).

*Case 1: both sisters are chosen.* Then $2$ more passengers are chosen from the other $6$:

$$\binom{6}{2} = 15 \text{ ways}.$$

*Case 2: neither sister is chosen.* Then all $4$ passengers are chosen from the other $6$:

$$\binom{6}{4} = 15 \text{ ways}.$$

The cases are mutually exclusive, so by the addition principle

$$\boxed{15 + 15 = 30 \text{ ways}}$$

Check: the total number of selections of $4$ from $8$ is $\binom84 = 70$; the selections that separate the sisters (exactly one of them chosen) number $2\binom63 = 40$, and $70 - 40 = 30$. Correct.

(Remark: if the question were read as "the two sisters must both be among the four chosen", the count would be only Case 1, i.e. $15$; the usual reading of "must not be separated" allows the sisters to be left behind together as well, which gives $30$.)
